newsitem.title: USA: Sony names new management team for studio.
newsitem.headline: Sony names new management team for studio.

text.p: Sony Corp. Tuesday named a new management team for its troubled Sony Pictures unit, and for the first time moved a Japanese executive into a top job at the studio.

The announcement comes after months of management turmoil that culminated last week in the resignation of Alan Levine as president of Sony Pictures Entertainment, the umbrella company for Columbia and Tri-Star Pictures.
The Japanese electronics giant said John Calley, President of United Artists Pictures, will join Sony Pictures Entertainment as president and chief operating officer, effective in early November.
Jeff Sagansky, executive vice president at Sony Corp. of America, will join Sony Pictures as co-president with responsibility for the management of the company under Calley.

Masayuki Nozoe, executive vice president for Sony Corp. of America, will become executive vice president for Sony Pictures, marking the first time a Japanese executive will play an active role in Sony's studio operations.
Sony said Calley, 66, will focus on the motion picture business and home video, with Sagansky focusing on television activities and international business.
Nozoe will be responsible for cross-company business development, liaison with corporate headquarters and technology management. All three executives will be based in Los Angeles.

"These are very important appointments for Sony Pictures Entertainment," said Nobuyuki Idei, Sony Corp. President and Chief Operating Officer. "John's vast experience and proven track record in the industry will be a tremendous asset to Sony."
Industry analysts said the decision to put Nozoe in the role of intermediary between Hollywood and Tokyo is a sign that Sony is going to assume more control over the studio.

"Clearly Tokyo is in charge," said Arthur Rockwell at Yaeger Capital Markets in Los Angeles. "I don't see them wanting to sell it off but obviously they have to get it in shape to do something with it."

Nozoe will work with Calley and Sagansky to improve relations with Tokyo and ensure the studio does not return to the days of former studio chiefs Peter Guber and Jon Peters, who spent millions of dollars on projects without much success, analysts said.
Shortly after Guber left in 1994, the studio took an embarrassing $3.2 billion write-off for its movie-making business.

Despite six consecutive quarters of profitability, Sony Pictures has struggled to achieve the same performance as its peers, with a big part of the profits coming from its television operations rather than the film unit.
This summer, the studio's biggest film, "The Cable Guy", opened to half-empty theaters despite a substantial marketing budget and a $20 million contract for comedian Jim Carrey.
The disappointing performance, coupled with lukewarm openings for "The Fan" and "Multiplicity" this summer, cost Sony studio boss Mark Canton his job last month and led to the departure of Levine.

The changes are part of a series of high-level departures this summer, including Marc Platt, who left his post as president of Sony's TriStar Pictures to move to Universal Pictures, and Lisa Henson, who stepped down as president of Sony's Columbia Pictures to form her own production company.
Sid Ganis, the head of Sony Pictures marketing unit, also left last summer.
The turmoil at Sony has prompted many to suggest the company may sell the troubled studio after amassing billions of dollars in losses since acquiring it for $3.4 billion in 1989.
But Idei said Sony intends to remain in Hollywood.

"This team represents a new vision and new direction for the studio," Idei said. "We are committed to the growth and success of Sony Pictures Entertainment and to making Sony the global entertainment and communications company of the future."
As head of Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Inc.'s United Artists studio, Calley played a key role in revitalizing the studio with hits such as "Goldeneye", "Birdcage" and "Leaving Las Vegas".
Sagansky, a former executive with CBS, now owned by Westinghouse Electric Corp., has been executive vice president since September 1994.
Nozoe has been executive vice president of Sony Corp. of America since February, mainly with responsibilities for new business development.
